extracted.intended_audience: mathematics and computer-science students and researchers writing term papers and research articles (audience of Don Knuth's mathematical writing course)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for writing clear, correct, and readable mathematical/CS exposition and term papers, covering grammar, notation, structure, style, and presentation for an academic audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct use of 'that' vs 'which'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'that' for defining/restrictive relative clauses and 'which' for non-defining/non-restrictive clauses; avoid unnecessary 'which' that signals nervous or unnatural diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strunk & White / Fowler guidance: If you can substitute 'that' for 'which', do it (Leslie Lamport's phrasing). Examples: "All the students that know..." vs "The exam, which took place..." Avoid gratuitous 'which'es; they hurt tone and may reduce readership. Note historical/usage exceptions (literary prose) and be aware readers indoctrinated by style guides may react to 'wicked whiches'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subheadings must be removable
rubrics_metrics.description: The main text should make sense if the titles of subsections are omitted; do not write sentences that depend on the subheading wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat subheadings as marginal/meta notes. Bad: "2. Contour Integration. This technique, invented by Cauchy, is used..." Better: "2. Contour Integration. The technique of integrating along curves..." — do not refer back to the heading as though it were part of the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms and symbols up front
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly define your terms and notation at the start (even basic ones), especially in fields like graph theory where usage varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what background your readers share; explicitly define ambiguous concepts (e.g., path vs simple path vs walk) and even symbols like '=' if they are nonstandard for your audience. Avoid assuming a universal usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise; shorten unwieldy definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer succinct definitions and statements; condense multi-part definitions when parts are unused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: collapse a long multi-line definition by removing unused subparts (e.g., omit W2 if unused). Principle: "Less is more." Shorter, clearer definitions reduce intimidation and aid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the same name for the same concept throughout (coordinate with co-authors), and avoid defining terms you never use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not call the same concept 'dominators' in one place and 'parents' in another. If co-authors disagree, pick one term. Also, don't introduce a symbol or name that then never appears—remove unused definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate tense for mathematical facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tense that reflects the timelessness of mathematical facts (algorithms and their worst-case complexities are typically stated in the present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Prefer "Gabow and Tarjan have shown..." rather than "had shown" when referring to a result about algorithms. Distinguish when past tense is appropriate (historical events or when referring to problems whose known complexity changed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation placement and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Place references so that sentences remain readable without them (parenthetical preferred); watch spacing and style conventions for citation markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like "Tarjan[Gab83]" (put a space before bracket) or "In [Smith 80] it was shown..." Prefer parentheses so the sentence reads sensibly without the reference. Consider mechanics of your citation style (names/dates vs numbering) and the effort required to renumber references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma usage reflects speech pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive commas; as a rough guide, put a comma where a speaker would naturally pause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example fix: "Our algorithm to recognize and label the graphs when given a directed graph, G, with distinguished vertex s, can be summarized as follows." — remove commas around 'G' and place a comma after 'graphs'. Overcommaing can harm flow and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose unambiguous words and terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer precise terminology to avoid ambiguity caused by words with multiple senses or unfortunate coincidences of context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change ambiguous 'loop' to 'self-loop'; avoid sentences like "the node x is left" (left = remaining vs left = past tense). Watch domain collisions (airplanes vs complex planes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simpler, clearer rules over contrived optimality
rubrics_metrics.description: When clarity is the goal, state a simple, easily understood rule rather than a more optimal but confusing restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If H0 already satisfies a condition, omit an unnecessary "j > 0" clause. Simpler statements are easier to read and less error-prone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pluralization and possessives of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Form plurals and possessives of symbols carefully to avoid typographic or readability problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of "the Hj's" (or Hjs) which can conflict with primes like H'j, write "each Hj is..." or invent another name if repeated heavily. Use apostrophes for genitives where appropriate ("Hj's descendants").

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compound adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyphens in compound adjectives to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write "one-vertex path" rather than "one vertex path." Hyphenation clarifies that the modifier applies to the noun as a unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer correct prepositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose prepositions that convey the intended mathematical relation precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use 'vertex at distance < d' rather than 'vertex of distance < d.' Small prepositional choices can alter meaning and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing and small formatting details
rubrics_metrics.description: Be attentive to small typographic/spacing conventions that affect readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: include a space in "4.3 (below)" rather than "4.3(below)". These details help the text look professional and read smoothly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect logical ordering of results and proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use lemmas/theorems before they are proved without clear indication; maintain the partial order of dependencies in exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must reference a later result, make it explicit so the reader doesn't suspect circular reasoning (using a result to prove itself). Structure proofs to respect dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ties/nonbreaking spaces to keep units together
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent harmful line breaks by using nonbreaking spaces (ties) between words and symbols that belong together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: put ties after 'dominates' in 'v dominates x and x dominates w' and between 'e' and 'is' in 'if e is ...' to avoid marring the flow or splitting identifiers across lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure examples as progressive sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of examples that build on one another is more useful than a set of unrelated examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design examples so that each extends the previous one, demonstrating increasing levels of complexity or generality (as in Haddad & Schäffer's paper).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-crowding the page with symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize cognitive load by not packing too many symbols or awkward symbol constructions on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a symbol becomes messy (e.g., Hj with primes, subscripts, etc.), consider renaming concepts or rephrasing to keep notation readable and elegant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone matters: small choices affect readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Tiny stylistic choices (word choice, pronoun use, punctuation) influence the reader's perception and willingness to keep reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent small improvements (e.g., correct which/that usage) increase attention and commitment from readers; many small mistakes accumulate to reduce impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use computer style/readability tools as aids, not authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Style and diction programs can provide readability grades and flag questionable phrasing, but their analysis is superficial and should prompt re-reading rather than blind changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readability scores are linear regressions based on words/sentence and syllables/word; aim to lower the grade level moderately but don't sacrifice necessary technical density. Diction lists may flag words ('gratuitous', 'due to') that are acceptable in mathematical context—interpret flags in domain context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of passive vs active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when passive constructions are natural in technical exposition and when active voice would improve clarity or engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style tools may label any sentence with a passive verb as passive even if subclauses contain it. Passive is common in technical writing (and sometimes appropriate), but excessive passivity can reduce readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise mathematical terminology and logical clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose mathematical terms accurately (e.g., differentiate factors vs terms) and write sentences whose logical flow can be unwound clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: don't conflate 'multiplicative factor' with 'multiplicative term'; rewrite sentences to make the logical relationships explicit, e.g., "Gabow and Tarjan have shown how to improve the algorithms by removing such a multiplicative factor..."
